story_text.value:
Hey HN, we recently open sourced our Consumer Agent Testing Tool to help teams iterate against proprietary assistants like Muse and Instinct. We built this to reduce our own frustrations with building an MCP/API for these agents to consume.

The problem: testing against these tools is hard! Agent memory + account statefulness make reproducibility, in the ways required for repeatable/reliable outcomes, between agents and the APIs/MCPs they interact with very challenging.

The solution: CATT lets devs test their services against a surrogate Muse or Instinct agent (not affiliated with either of these companies). Testers define starting conditions, approvals, and success conditions for their service's state. CATT then records the full interaction (incl. tool calls, responses) so it can diff what happened from what the agent reports. Runs can be tested in local builds or via CI, with or without LLM backing.

CATT is designed to emulate the important parts of personal assistant interactions. Its got:

- Tool calls and command-line tool access - Simulated approvals for service actions - Outcomes tracking and comparison - Optional MCP profile based on an unofficial Muse template

There are limitations to how much we know about different assistant specific behaviors so the tool labels its assumptions as `documented`, `unofficial`, `assumed` or `unknown` for developer review. We'll do our best to keep the tool updated as new insights about the internal workings of these assistants come to light. It is an area of active research and interest, a good example is this recent report on how Instinct uses Exa for web search [0].

Are you building a connector or MCP? If yes, we'd like to hear from you! Have you had assistants behave incoherently, use stale information, or procalim success without evidence? What else should we add tests for?

The best way to get started is...to point your coding assistant at the repo and ask it to integrate the tool with your CI or local testing pipeline!

Hope it's helpful!

[0]: https://www.sunbeam.ai/thoughts/instinct-is-using-exa-for-we...

story_text.value:
time says a command took 3.8 seconds... whytime tells you where those seconds went:

  $ sudo whytime -- sh -c 'sleep 0.5; dd … oflag=dsync; curl -s -o /dev/null https://speed.cloudflare.com/…'
  wall 3.83s
    47%  blocked on network: speed.cloudflare.com:443 (1 connection)
    34%  fsync on ~/.cache
    13%  timer sleep (sleep)
     4%  on-CPU (curl)
     2%  other
The lines always add up to 100%. When the command waits on a child or another thread, whytime follows whoever woke it up, so a shell waiting on curl is charged to the network wait curl was stuck on. The top line is what you'd have to make faster.

It can also draw a flamegraph.

Uses eBPF (Linux 5.18+)

story_text.value:
Hi HNers,

About a month ago, a post entitled "Why is Google still serving dodgy ads" gathered quite a few comments. My project to remediate this problem was already well underway, but it only just launched this Tuesday, so I’d be very grateful if original participants could take it for a spin. The only requirement is an email address for the sending of major product update notifications. You’re welcome to use a throwaway account in any case.

On to the meat: BidBouncer is a free (it’s still in beta), daily-updated URL blocklist of egregious ads. Installation and updates are taken care of from inside Google Ad Manager through a bookmarklet – full source provided, for obvious reasons. Coverage should be at least adequate.

If BidBouncer gets traction, updates will be fully automated; subscriptions will cost a ludicrously low price, as I am well aware that everything from the data to the client-side code is fully exposed and there is no moat. I’d rather undercut myself than have someone else repackage my work; I also wish to help as many fellow tiny publishers as possible to uphold high ad quality standards.

Feedback welcome, be it good or bad.

title.value: Show HN: Daily-updated bad ads blocklist for publishers

story_text.value:
I know there are many dictation apps out there, but I built one myself anyways based on my custom needs. Since OpenAI dictation is so good, my previous workflow would be speaking to ChatGPT UI and pasting a default prompt to turn my speech into a well formatted prompt

Now I just hold a key (Fn for me), talk, let go, and the text gets pasted wherever the cursor is, mostly Claude Code in the terminal. The default prompt part became "Modes" where you write the instructions once (clean it up, translate to English, etc) and the transcript goes through an OpenAI model before it's pasted.

It uses your own OpenAI key and calls their API directly, no server in between. My daily spend is usually around US$ 0.15.

It's cloud only, so if you want local models Handy or VoiceInk are better picks. No signed release yet, you build it with Xcode using one script. MIT licensed.

title.value: Show HN: Murmur, open-source push-to-talk dictation for Mac (BYO OpenAI key)

story_text.value:
What do you get when you combine Space Invaders, classic literature, and ascii? Txt Invaders!

https://txtinvaders.com/

I've been obsessing over "fluid text" effect and decided to combine this with two things I love - literature and retro games (in this case Space Invaders).

You play against a backdrop of classic literature excerpts (think Pride and Prejudice). As your ship moves <- / -> and as you fire the lasers at the invading aliens, there is this smooth ripple effect around the characters and words. Defeating the wave of aliens awards you with a beautiful quote from one of the books. You just have to see it for yourselves.

Enjoy!

story_text.value:
Hi HN, I have been building OpenPanopticon for almost a year and finally wanted to share it with the world.

It pulls data from across the internet and shows it in a single combined geopraphic view. Think of it as the closest thing we can get to Enemy of the State or Palantir-esque synthesis of disparate date sources.

There is a demo linked on the Github site with read-only data for New York in addition to some screenshots showing off some of the data I have seen. You can combine sources like Shodan, ADSB, and traffic cameras to get a real sense of how the physical and informational worlds interact.

Cheers and happy hunting.

story_text.value:
Plango is a Mac native security suite for anyone running AI coding tools. It works by running a custom local security model that evaluates threats against the lethal trifecta (data access, communication, exposure).

Some cool features: - Restrict Agent access by type of data (ssh keys, env files) or finder tags (finally a good reason to use the color tags in finder). - On device security model, but can switch to another local agent or bring your own key. - Review your Mac's privacy and access, apps, startup & extensions. - Automatically move env secrets into keychain. - Network blocks/allow lists, see what apps and agents are accessing. Stop them from data exfil. - Check skills and plugins for bad behavior. - Create custom rules for all of these things. - Log every action, request, block etc in an easy dashboard. - Vuln scan of all projects on your Mac.

About us: I'm Fred, long term hacker first time shower. My co-founder Rich and I care about privacy, security and believe that AI software development is the future. We have two decades of combined experience in cyber, NLP and AI and are working on this tool full time. Given how fast cyber is evolving we're pushing changes to this on a daily basis.

Please download and trial for free! We're here to answer any questions about the app or cyber/AI.

title.value: Show HN: Secure your AI agents on Mac

story_text.value:
Hi HN, I'm Anish. I built Mnemolith because the AI coding tools I use (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex) either forget my project between sessions, or remember things that quietly stopped being true. Tell the agent "we use Postgres", migrate to MySQL two weeks later, and it keeps building on the old fact.

How it works:

- It's an MCP server, so Claude Code, Cursor and Codex share one memory per project (keyed by the git repo). - When the agent saves a memory, it can link it to the files it depends on. Mnemolith stores each file's git blob hash. If the file's contents change (committed or not), the memory is set aside and flagged for review, so the agent stops relying on it. - A local dashboard shows what the agent remembers, where each memory came from (tool, session, file versions), and its full history. You can confirm a memory is still true, or retire it and say what's true now. - Contradictions are judged by the agent, not by a similarity threshold. In my calibration, "we use Postgres" vs "we migrated to MySQL" only scored 0.30 similarity, so a threshold can't tell a contradiction from an unrelated fact. - Current memories can sync into a managed section of AGENTS.md / CLAUDE.md, so they get reviewed in PRs.

Under the hood it runs on an engine I wrote from scratch in Java: a Redis-compatible server with a built-in memory model and an HNSW vector index. Embeddings run locally (all-MiniLM-L6-v2). Everything stays on your machine.

It's early (v0.2.1). There's no team sync yet beyond the AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md files, and it needs Java 11+ (it downloads a private copy if you don't have one).

I'd really like feedback, especially from people running coding agents on real codebases. What does your agent keep getting wrong?

title.value: Show HN: Mnemolith – AI coding memory that goes stale when your code changes
